To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Twitter was a useful source of information during the H1N 1 Pandemic and it was possible to use thematic analysis as a method to study the content of tweets.
the H1N 1 pandemic was communicated on social media in eight key themes.

Twitter users communicated about the H1NIn pandemic of 2009 by using humour and sarcasm to make light of the situation, they were concerned about the health of others and the potential for the virus to spread, they were concerned that pigs and pork may be able to host or transmit the virus, and they were interested in receiving and sharing health information.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the communication of information about a pandemic, but it also provides an innovative approach to studying the use of social media platforms in general.
the role of Twitter as a medium for the communication of health information, and how the medium can be used to gain insight into public views and attitudes towards health information.
the role of social media in the context of public health and the potential of social media to influence public health policy and practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Twitter users communicated about H1N1 in a way which was informative, emotional, and humorous.
Twitter can provide a rich and detailed source of data for health professionals, researchers and health information and library professionals.
Twitter users communicated a variety of information and emotions about the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, including a belief that pigs and pigs could host and/or spread the virus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the thematic analysis of Twitter content can be a valuable tool for health information professionals.
the methodological approach we utilised provided a more in-depth understanding of the communication of users about the H1N 1 pandemic.
it provides a novel methodological approach for analysing user communication about infectious diseases on Twitter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social media platforms can be used to gain a deeper understanding of how users communicate about a disease outbreak.
health organisations and libraries need to be aware of the role that social media can play in the dissemination of health information.

indepth methods can provide valuable insights into how users communicate on social media platforms, which in turn can help inform health information professionals about the communication needs of users during disease outbreaks.
